rows.name: the Peruvian Armed Forces
rows.note: Presence only: articles 273, 275 and 278 of the 1979 constitution identify the Army, Navy and Air Force, the president's command, an internal-order role during emergencies, and subordination to constitutional power. This establishes the institution in 1990, not an inevitable coup, exceptional starting hostility or a future event. The model's Army pillar represents the conventional armed services together. Existing personnel, party shares, civilian-control and funding data remain unchanged.

rows.name: the Guatemalan Army
rows.note: Presence only: the Inter-American Commission on Human Rights documents the Army and loyal armed forces suppressing the May 1989 coup attempt; its January-February 1990 visit also distinguishes the Government and Army in peace negotiations. Both military factions and forces loyal to constitutional government existed. No coup date, factional support or special loyalty penalty is encoded; existing personnel, party shares and funding data remain unchanged.

rows.name: the Honduran Armed Forces
rows.note: Presence only: the US Department of State's report for 1990, archived by ecoi.net, describes the elected civilian government and the Armed Forces' substantial legal and institutional autonomy. The report covers a year, not a measured opening loyalty score. The Army pillar represents the conventional military institution; it is not inferred solely from the personnel series, which can include paramilitary forces. Existing authoritarianism, personnel, party shares and funding data remain unchanged.
